transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Abortion rights, voter ID, and congressional redistricting
are among the nearly 150 state ballot questions
facing voters this election day.
We could see record high turnout for the midterms.
NPR's Domenico Montanaro says Latino voters
will be a key demographic in several races.
Latinos have soured on President Trump in the second term.
His approval ratings with the group are low,
and they make up large portions of lots of congressional districts.
Particularly important to watch is going to be South Florida and South Texas.
Trump won over many Latinos in those places in the 2024 presidential election,
but because of the cost of living and harsh deportation tactics,
there are signs they are either going to swing back to Democrats or stay home.
Either way, Democrats need to flip three seats to win control of the House,
and there are at least 20 targeted districts where Latinos make up
at least one in five people, making them a critical group to watch.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
Democrats are hoping to retake control of Congress from Republicans come January.
Some of the most closely watched contests, Senate races in Texas, Michigan, and Alaska.
Another consequential Senate race is in Iowa,
where Iowa Public Radio's Sheila Bremmer says voters are also deciding on their next governor.
More than three dozen people lined up to vote at East High School in Sioux City
at seven this morning, a bigger crowd than usual, according to poll workers.
Among them was Cindy Tutahoe.
I think this is an important election.
Mid-term usually isn't, but I think it is this year.
Republican Ashley Hinson faces Democrat Josh Turek
in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races.
Democrats hope to flip the seat to help regain control of the Senate.
The governor's race could bring another political shift.
Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lane are competing for an office
Republicans have held for more than 15 years.
For NPR News, I'm Sheila Bremmer in Sioux City.
President Trump says he has struck a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
to halt $4 billion in USAID to Israel and replace it with weapons sales.
But NPR's Lauren Fair reports from Tel Aviv
Netanyahu's office has not confirmed a new arrangement.
Israeli media are reporting the country's defense and finance ministries
were caught by surprise at President Trump's announcement.
It's been a week since inconclusive elections here,
with Prime Minister Netanyahu falling short of a parliamentary majority.
His main challenger, Gadi Isinkot, says the fact that Israelis are learning about this change
from the media shows they can no longer rely on Netanyahu and should replace him.
Another opposition leader, Yair Golan, says a "responsible" prime minister
would fight to increase American aid, not dismantle it.
The current framework for such aid had been scheduled to expire by 2028.
In recent months, Netanyahu has said he wants to wean Israel off USAID, but hasn't said when.
Lauren Frier, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
This is NPR News.
Voting machine programmings blame for ballot-scanning problems
in New York's Westchester County today.
However, officials say voting continues.
At the Supreme Court, the focus was on a Colorado program that seeks to provide an education
and full funding for all four-year-olds in the state.
Here's NPR's Nina Totenberg.
While the Catholic Church initially supported the program and Catholic charity still participates,
the Archdiocese of Denver and two Catholic parishes are suing the state for its anti-discrimination law.
The objectors contend that the law violates the Constitution's guarantee to the free exercise of religion,
but specifically the church contends that it should be able to reject students whose families are gay or trans,
and still receive funding from the state.
Multiple religious schools still participate in the universal pre-K program.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
Getting around on an electric bike are scooters increasingly popular in urban areas,
and as one study now finds, more dangerous for kids.
And here's Rachel Karaslin with more.
Brain injuries were twice as common among kids injured on e-bikes and e-scooters compared to their non-motorized counterparts.
And 8% of patients with e-bike injuries had major problems or needed ICU-level care.
That's twice the rate of high-severity injuries versus non-motorized bikes.
The data comes from the medical records of over 13,000 young people treated for bike,
scooter, and skateboard injuries at six large U.S. pediatric hospitals over the course of three years.
Rachel Carlson, NPR News.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Ballot questions on abortion, voter ID, and redistricting face voters in nearly 150 state measures
NPR's Domenico Montanaro says Latino voters could be decisive in several midterm races
Democrats hope to retake Congress, with key Senate races in Texas, Michigan, and Alaska
Iowa voters turn out in larger-than-usual numbers in Sioux City for midterms
Iowa Senate race pits Ashley Hinson against Josh Turek; governor's race features Sand and Lane
Trump says he struck a deal with Netanyahu to halt $4 billion in USAID to Israel
Netanyahu's office has not confirmed the new U.S.-Israel aid arrangement; Israeli ministries were surprised
Voting machine programming blamed for ballot-scanning problems in Westchester County, New York
Supreme Court hears case on Colorado universal pre-K program and Catholic church's discrimination objections
Study finds brain injuries twice as common in kids hurt on e-bikes and e-scooters
